oggetti/leggenda-pianeti/cosa: Why the planets bear the names of the gods of Rome, and who had named them before.
oggetti/leggenda-pianeti/paragrafi/0/tes: The ancients looked at the sky every night. They noticed that almost all the stars stay fixed in relation to one another. Five lights, however, move slowly among the constellations. The Greeks called them planetes, meaning "wanderers". That's where the word planet comes from.
oggetti/leggenda-pianeti/paragrafi/1/tes: The first people to follow the planets carefully were the astronomers of Mesopotamia. Each planet was linked to a god. Marduk, the king of the gods of Babylon, was Jupiter. Ishtar, goddess of love and war, was Venus. Nergal, god of war and plagues, was red Mars. Nabu, god of scribes, was Mercury. Saturn was linked to Ninurta.
oggetti/leggenda-pianeti/paragrafi/2/tes: At first the Greeks used descriptive names. Mars was Pyroeis, "the fiery one". Saturn was Phainon, "the shining one". Then they took up the Babylonian idea and chose gods similar to their own: Zeus, Aphrodite, Ares, Hermes and Cronus. Venus, seen in the morning and in the evening, had two names for a long time: Phosphorus and Hesperus. It's said that it was Pythagoras or Parmenides who realised it was a single body.
oggetti/leggenda-pianeti/paragrafi/3/tes: The Romans translated once again, using their own gods. Zeus became Jupiter, Aphrodite Venus, Ares Mars, Hermes Mercury, Cronus Saturn. These are the names we still use today. The choices have a logic of their own. Mercury, the swift messenger, is the fastest planet. Mars, the god of war, is the colour of blood. Jupiter, the king, is the brightest after Venus. Saturn, the oldest god, is the slowest of all.
oggetti/leggenda-urano-nettuno/nome: The planet that was meant to be called George
oggetti/leggenda-urano-nettuno/cosa: How Uranus and Neptune got their names, after long arguments.
oggetti/leggenda-urano-nettuno/paragrafi: On 13 March 1781 William Herschel, a musician and astronomer in England, saw a strange dot in his telescope. At first he thought it was a comet. Instead it was a new planet, the first discovered with a telescope. It needed a name, and that had never happened before.

Herschel wanted to thank his king, George III. So he proposed Georgium Sidus, "George's Star". In England people liked the name. In the rest of Europe, much less so. In France many simply called it "Herschel".

The German astronomer Johann Bode proposed Uranus. In Greek myth Uranus, the Sky, is the father of Cronus, that is, of Saturn. And Saturn is the father of Jupiter. So the family went up one generation. The name caught on little by little. The British only officially adopted it around 1850. In 1789 the chemist Klaproth named a new element uranium, precisely in honour of the planet.

Neptune was discovered in 1846 in Berlin by Johann Galle. Galle searched at the spot indicated by the calculations of the Frenchman Urbain Le Verrier. Various names were proposed, such as Janus and Oceanus. For a while Le Verrier even backed the name "Le Verrier". In the end Neptune won, the Roman god of the sea, to keep to the tradition of the ancient gods.

Pluto was discovered in 1930. The name was suggested by an eleven-year-old girl from Oxford, Venetia Burney. Pluto is the god of the underworld, fitting for a distant, dark body. Since 2006 Pluto has been considered a dwarf planet.
oggetti/leggenda-settimana/nome: A week written in the sky
oggetti/leggenda-settimana/cosa: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday: the days are named after the seven wandering lights.
oggetti/leggenda-settimana/paragrafi/0/t: For the ancients there were seven bodies moving among the stars: the Sun, the Moon and the five planets visible to the naked eye. Each day of the week was dedicated to one of them. This custom spread through the Roman Empire between the first and second centuries AD.
oggetti/leggenda-settimana/paragrafi/1/t: In Italian, lunedì (Monday) is the day of the Moon (Luna). Martedì (Tuesday) belongs to Mars (Marte), mercoledì (Wednesday) to Mercury (Mercurio). Giovedì (Thursday) belongs to Jupiter (Giove), venerdì (Friday) to Venus (Venere). Sabato (Saturday) and domenica (Sunday) have changed over time. Sabato comes from the Hebrew shabbat, the day of rest, but it used to be Saturn's day. Domenica comes from the Latin dies Dominicus, the Lord's day, but it used to be the day of the Sun.
oggetti/leggenda-settimana/paragrafi/2/t: The ancients ranked the seven bodies from slowest to fastest: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon. Each hour of the day was entrusted to one of them, in turn. The body of the first hour gave its name to the whole day. With 24 hours in a day, the turn jumps forward in a regular way. And out comes exactly the sequence of our week. The Roman historian Cassius Dio explains it.
oggetti/leggenda-settimana/paragrafi/3/t: The same planets around the world

In English the days of the Sun (Sunday), the Moon (Monday) and Saturn (Saturday) remain. The other days took Germanic gods similar to the Roman ones: Tiw for Mars, Woden for Mercury, Thor for Jupiter, Frigg for Venus. In Japanese, too, the days follow the seven bodies. There, though, the planets are named after the Chinese elements: fire, water, wood, metal and earth.
oggetti/leggenda-stelle-arabe/cosa: Aldebaran, Rigel, Vega: a journey of names from Greece to Baghdad and then to Europe.
oggetti/leggenda-stelle-arabe/paragrafi/: In the second century AD the astronomer Ptolemy, in Alexandria in Egypt, wrote a great work. It contained more than a thousand stars in 48 constellations. The stars had hardly any proper names. They were described by their position: "the one in the foot", "the one on the tail".

In the ninth century Ptolemy's work was translated into Arabic in Baghdad, under the name Almagest. In 964 the Persian astronomer al-Sufi wrote the Book of Fixed Stars. He combined Ptolemy's descriptions with the names the Arab peoples had given the stars for centuries. In this way many descriptions became real names.

Aldebaran comes from al-dabaran, "the one who follows", because it seems to chase the Pleiades. Rigel comes from rijl, "foot": it's the foot of the giant Orion. Deneb comes from dhanab, "tail", the tail of the bird Cygnus. Altair is "the flying eagle". Vega comes from al-nasr al-waqi, "the swooping eagle".

In the Middle Ages Arabic books were translated into Latin, especially in Spain. The copyists often didn't know Arabic, and the names got distorted. Betelgeuse probably comes from yad al-jawza, "the hand of al-Jawza", a figure of the Arabic sky. A copyist misread a letter and wrote a "b" instead of a "y". Later people thought it meant "the armpit", but that explanation arose after the mistake.
Not all of them are Arabic

Some names come from Greek or Latin. Antares is Greek and means "rival of Ares", that is, of Mars, because of its red colour. Sirius is Greek; Spica is Latin and means "ear of grain". Since 2016 the International Astronomical Union has made the proper names of hundreds of stars official.
oggetti/leggenda-sirio/nome: Sirius, the Nile and the dog days
oggetti/leggenda-sirio/cosa: The brightest star in the sky heralded the flooding of the Nile and the heat of summer.
oggetti/leggenda-sirio/paragrafi/0/testo: For the ancient Egyptians Sirius was the goddess Sopdet, whom the Greeks called Sothis. For part of the year Sirius stays hidden in the Sun's glare. Then one summer day it reappears at dawn, low in the east. At about that time the Nile flood began, making the fields fertile. So the return of Sirius was a celebration and marked the new year.
oggetti/leggenda-sirio/paragrafi/1/testo: For the Greeks Sirius was the brightest star in Canis Major, the Great Dog. The dog followed the hunter Orion across the sky. Homer, in the Iliad, already calls it "Orion's dog" and says it brings fever to mortals. Some ancient authors also tell of Laelaps, a dog that never let its prey escape. The name Sirius may come from a Greek word meaning "scorching", but its origin isn't certain.
oggetti/leggenda-sirio/paragrafi/2/testo: The Romans called Sirius Canicula, "the little dog". They noticed that Sirius rose together with the Sun on the hottest days of the year. They thought its fire added to the Sun's. This gave rise to the Italian word canicola, the sultry summer heat, known in English as the "dog days".
oggetti/leggenda-sirio/paragrafi/3/testo: The summer heat doesn't depend on Sirius but on the tilt of the Earth. What's more, the sky changes slowly over the centuries. Today in Italy Sirius reappears at dawn around mid-August, later than in ancient times. But the name canicola has stuck.
oggetti/leggenda-pleiadi/nome: The Seven Sisters around the world
oggetti/leggenda-pleiadi/cosa: A small group of stars that almost every people on Earth has told stories about.
oggetti/leggenda-pleiadi/paragrafi/0/tes: For the Greeks the Pleiades were seven sisters, daughters of the Titan Atlas and of Pleione. Their names were Maia, Electra, Taygete, Alcyone, Celaeno, Sterope and Merope. The hunter Orion chased them for years. So Zeus turned them into doves and then into stars. The Greek farmer Hesiod used their rising and setting to know when to reap and when to plough.
oggetti/leggenda-pleiadi/paragrafi/1/tes: With the naked eye you can easily see six, not seven. The ancients had an explanation. According to Ovid, Merope hides out of shame, because she married a mortal. According to other tales it's Electra who covers her face, in grief at the fall of Troy.
oggetti/leggenda-pleiadi/paragrafi/2/tes: In Japan the Pleiades are called Subaru, a word meaning "to gather together". It's also the name of a car maker, which has the stars in its logo. In New Zealand the Māori call them Matariki. When they reappear at dawn, in the middle of the southern winter between June and July, the Māori new year begins. Since 2022 Matariki has been a public holiday in New Zealand.
oggetti/leggenda-pleiadi/paragrafi/3/tes: Many Aboriginal Australian peoples also see a group of sisters in the Pleiades. In their stories the sisters flee from a man who chases them across the desert. In many versions the pursuer is right there in the stars of Orion. It's surprising: peoples very far apart tell a very similar story. Nobody knows for sure why.
oggetti/leggenda-orsa-maggiore/nome: A bear, a plough, seven sages
oggetti/leggenda-orsa-maggiore/cosa: The seven most famous stars of the northern sky have a thousand different stories.
oggetti/leggenda-orsa-maggiore/paragrafi: For the Greeks the Great Bear was Callisto, a nymph who followed the goddess Artemis. Zeus fell in love with her and a son was born, Arcas. According to Ovid, jealous Juno turned Callisto into a bear. Years later Arcas, out hunting, was about to strike his mother without recognising her. Zeus stopped the arrow and took them both up into the sky.
The bear that never takes a bath

Juno wasn't happy to see Callisto among the stars. She asked the gods of the sea never to let her bathe in the Ocean. That's why, Ovid tells us, the Great Bear never sets below the horizon. Indeed, from Italy we see it circling the Pole Star all year round. Nearby is Arcturus, whose Greek name means "guardian of the bear".

Many peoples saw not a bear but a wagon. The Romans called the seven stars Septentriones, "the seven oxen" pulling the plough. From this word comes the Italian settentrione, meaning the north. In English the same stars are the Plough or the Big Dipper.

In India the seven stars are the Saptarishi, the seven sages of ancient tradition. One of them, Vasishtha, is the star Mizar. Next to him shines a fainter little star, Alcor. She is Arundhati, his faithful wife. At some Hindu weddings she is still pointed out to the bride and groom as an example of faithfulness.
oggetti/leggenda-orione-scorpione/nome: Orion and the Scorpion, enemies for ever
oggetti/leggenda-orione-scorpione/cosa: Why the hunter and the scorpion are never in the sky together.
oggetti/leggenda-orione-scorpione/paragr: Orion was a giant, a mighty hunter. According to one of the ancient tales he was also very proud. He boasted that he could kill every animal on Earth. The Earth, offended, sent a scorpion against him. The little creature stung him and killed him.

The gods took both Orion and the Scorpion up into the sky. But they placed them on opposite sides, so they would never meet again. And that's exactly how it is. When Scorpius rises in the east, Orion sets in the west. Orion rules the winter nights, Scorpius the summer ones.

Ancient myths often come in several versions. In some, Orion dies from an arrow shot by Artemis, tricked by her brother Apollo. In others it's the goddess herself who sends the scorpion. These stories are told by writers such as Eratosthenes and Hyginus, who collected the tales of the constellations.

The two constellations have something in common. Both have a great red star. In Orion it's Betelgeuse, on the hunter's shoulder. In Scorpius it's Antares, the heart of the creature. Its name means "rival of Mars", because its colour is like the planet's.
oggetti/leggenda-zodiaco/nome: The zodiac and the thirteenth sign
oggetti/leggenda-zodiaco/cosa: The twelve signs come from Babylon, but the Sun also passes through a thirteenth constellation.
oggetti/leggenda-zodiaco/paragrafi/0/tes: During the year the Sun seems to pass in front of different constellations. The Moon and the planets follow more or less the same path too. The astronomers of Babylon watched this band of sky for centuries. As early as around 1000 BC its constellations were listed in a collection of tablets called MUL.APIN.
oggetti/leggenda-zodiaco/paragrafi/1/tes: Around the fifth century BC the Babylonians divided the path of the Sun into twelve equal parts. Many of the names are today's: the Bull, the Twins, the Lion, the Scorpion. Others changed. The Ram was originally "the hired labourer". Capricorn was a creature half goat and half fish, and it has kept its tail. The Greeks adopted the system and called it the zodiac, "circle of little animals".
oggetti/leggenda-zodiaco/paragrafi/2/tes: The Earth's axis wobbles slowly like a spinning top, making one turn about every 26,000 years. The Greek Hipparchus discovered this in the second century BC. That's why the horoscope signs no longer match the real constellations. Today, when the horoscope says Aries, the Sun is in front of Pisces.
oggetti/leggenda-zodiaco/paragrafi/3/tes: In 1930 astronomers fixed the official boundaries of the constellations. It turned out that the Sun, between late November and mid-December, also passes through Ophiuchus, "the serpent bearer". In myth he is Asclepius, the physician who could bring the dead back to life. Zeus struck him with a thunderbolt for this, then placed him among the stars. Astrology doesn't count him, but astronomers do.
oggetti/leggenda-via-lattea/nome: A river of milk in the sky
oggetti/leggenda-via-lattea/cosa: A goddess's milk, a silver river, a pilgrims' road: our galaxy as told by the peoples of the world.
oggetti/leggenda-via-lattea/paragrafi/0/: For the Greeks the Milky Way was born from a drop of milk. Zeus put the baby Heracles to the breast of the goddess Hera while she slept, to make him immortal. Hera woke up and pushed him away. The milk spilt across the sky. The Greeks called it galaxias kyklos, "circle of milk". That's where our word galaxy comes from.
oggetti/leggenda-via-lattea/paragrafi/1/: In China the Milky Way is the River of Heaven. On one side is the star Vega, the Weaver Girl. On the other is Altair, the Cowherd, the young man who grazes the oxen. The two loved each other, but the river keeps them apart. Once a year, on the seventh day of the seventh month, magpies form a bridge and they meet. In Japan the same festival is called Tanabata.
oggetti/leggenda-via-lattea/paragrafi/2/: In Spain and other parts of Europe, folk tradition called the Milky Way the Way of St James (Camino de Santiago). It seemed to show pilgrims the road to Santiago de Compostela. It's a folk name, not an ancient myth, but it's still very widespread today.
oggetti/leggenda-via-lattea/paragrafi/3/: The Emu and the dark animals

Some peoples looked at the dark patches, not the stars. Many Aboriginal Australians see a great emu in the dark clouds of the Milky Way. Its head is near the Southern Cross. Its position in the evening sky shows when emus lay their eggs. The Inca and their descendants in the Andes also see dark figures in the Mayu, the celestial river: a llama, a toad, a snake and a fox.
oggetti/leggenda-nubi-magellano/cosa: The Magellanic Clouds and the Southern Cross, the wonders of the southern sky.
oggetti/leggenda-nubi-magellano/paragraf: The Magellanic Clouds are two small galaxies close to our own. They can never be seen from Italy. The first person to write about them may have been the Persian astronomer al-Sufi, in 964. He reported that from southern Arabia you could see a patch called al-Bakr, "the white ox".
The Italians and the new stars

European navigators saw these skies at the beginning of the 16th century. Amerigo Vespucci, in his letters, speaks of light and dark patches near the south pole. In 1515 the Florentine Andrea Corsali wrote to Giuliano de' Medici. He described two little clouds and a "croce maravigliosa" ("marvellous cross"), and made a drawing of it. It's one of the first European descriptions of the Southern Cross.

Antonio Pigafetta, from Vicenza, travelled around the world with Ferdinand Magellan between 1519 and 1522. In his diary he described the two clouds. Later they were called the Magellanic Clouds, in honour of that voyage.

Two thousand years ago the Southern Cross could also be seen from the Mediterranean, low on the horizon. Ptolemy included its stars in the constellation Centaurus. Then the slow movement of the Earth's axis hid it from our skies. Today it's on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Samoa and Papua New Guinea.
The compass of the southern peoples

For Polynesian navigators the Southern Cross helped them find south on the open sea. Hawaiians call it Hanaiakamalama. For many Aboriginal Australians the dark cloud next to the Cross, the Coalsack, is the head of the celestial Emu.
oggetti/leggenda-andromeda/nome: Andromeda, the princess and the galaxy
oggetti/leggenda-andromeda/cosa: A Greek myth with a whole family in the sky, and a little cloud that was another universe.
oggetti/leggenda-andromeda/paragrafi/0/t: A queen who was far too vain

Cepheus was king of Ethiopia and Cassiopeia was his wife. Cassiopeia boasted that she was more beautiful than the Nereids, the sea nymphs. Poseidon, offended, sent a sea monster to ravage the coasts. An oracle said that only a sacrifice could save the kingdom. Their daughter Andromeda was chained to a rock, to await the monster.
oggetti/leggenda-andromeda/paragrafi/1/t: Perseus was flying home after killing Medusa. He saw Andromeda, killed the monster and married her. In the Greek tales Perseus flies with the winged sandals of Hermes. The image of Perseus riding the winged horse Pegasus came later: in the ancient myth Pegasus is the horse of Bellerophon. Pegasus, however, was born from the very blood of Medusa.
oggetti/leggenda-andromeda/paragrafi/2/t: The whole family in the sky

The gods placed all the main characters among the stars: Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Andromeda, Perseus and the monster, Cetus the Whale. Cassiopeia sits on her throne. As she circles the pole, she sometimes ends up upside down. According to the ancients, this was a punishment for her vanity. In Perseus shines Algol, whose Arabic name means "the demon's head": it's the head of Medusa.
oggetti/leggenda-andromeda/paragrafi/3/t: In 964 the Persian astronomer al-Sufi noticed a "little cloud" in the constellation Andromeda. It's the oldest known description of the Andromeda Galaxy. For centuries people thought it was a nearby mist, inside our own Milky Way.
oggetti/leggenda-andromeda/paragrafi/4/t: In 1923 Edwin Hubble found some variable stars called Cepheids in that cloud. Their name comes from the star Delta Cephei, in the very constellation of King Cepheus. Thanks to them Hubble measured the distance. Andromeda was extremely far away: a whole galaxy, now estimated at about 2.5 million light years. It's the most distant object that can be seen with the naked eye.
